items.summary: Signal announced new protections designed to stop the AI assistants built into iOS 27 (Siri's Onscreen Awareness) and supported Android devices (Google's Gemini Intelligence) from capturing private conversations while performing tasks for users. The change follows a May 2025 feature that blocked Microsoft's Recall screenshot-capturing capability on Windows 11, with Signal president Meredith Whittaker stating in a blog post that the company would take similar measures to restrict agentic systems embedded deep in operating systems where apps have limited protection options. Signal described OS-level features as able to capture chat content directly from the app screen, placing sensitive data outside its control and exposing all conversation participants; engineers reportedly spent months reverse-engineering how AI systems access app data to block verified extraction pathways. The protections are activated automatically when possible without specific version numbers, with iOS users directed to Settings > App Security to confirm Block Siri AI is enabled and macOS 27 users advised to add the app to the Excluded Apps list under System Settings > Siri. Signal warned that screenshot-blocking on iOS also prevents legitimate screenshots by all users, and noted it currently cannot provide any screenshot protection for macOS, while cautioning that AI agents remain an existential threat capable of accessing conversations through undisclosed methods such as files, notifications, and APIs. The company called on Apple, Google, and Microsoft to fully disclose access mechanisms and give developers a clear way to opt out of AI access across screens, files, notifications, and APIs.
items.title: Signal Adds Protections to Block Siri and Gemini From Capturing Chats on iOS 27 and Android

items.summary: In a November 2026 podcast interview about his book Platform Extractivism: Data Work and the People Powering Artificial Intelligence (University of California Press, 2026), Yale assistant professor Julián Posada argues that artificial intelligence's promise of freedom from work has not materialized for most people. The central finding is that AI systems—facial recognition, content moderation, self-driving vehicles—are trained on invisible data-labeling labor performed largely by Venezuelan workers during the country's economic collapse and COVID-19 pandemic. Posada explains this concentration through three factors: Venezuela's hyperinflation (which pushed unemployed citizens toward dollar-denominated platform income), inherited infrastructure such as government-built Canaima computers, and a flexible gig-style model requiring only accounts rather than facilities like traditional business-process outsourcing did. He notes the industry was focused on computer vision tasks—tagging images, roads, and objects—for supervised learning in the late 2019 to early 2020s, before shifting toward large language models that required English-language skills and redirected work to Kenya, the Philippines, and India. Posada describes "epistemic dominance," where workers are forced by precarious conditions to encode knowledge from top-down instructions—such as applying a US census racial taxonomy or binary hate-speech labels grounded in First Amendment standards—that imposed foreign frameworks on Latin American workers; dissent typically results in being kicked out of tasks, banned, or unpaid. He documents worker organizing through closed Telegram and WhatsApp groups that provided trusted currency brokers (using digital currencies like AirTM), shared platform exploits, and insurance against scams, though he notes many such groups likely disbanded when Venezuela's situation improved after the Russian invasion of Ukraine. Posada frames gig-style terms as spreading to high-paid sectors like medicine—citing Scale AI/Remotasks' Outlier recruiting cardiologists at roughly $180 an hour under identical terms copied from Remotasks—and warns that rising productivity has not reduced unemployment or trickled down wages in a K-shaped economy. He acknowledges the population is invisible and uncountable, with families sharing accounts and minors using grandparents' identities to authenticate them; he attributes his estimates of global division of labor to web traffic analysis rather than firm employment figures. Posada expresses hope that regulation will come from destination countries like the United States—referencing a prior USAID policy for decent conditions across the AI data pipeline—and stresses both top-down regulation and bottom-up worker organizing remain essential, while noting he could not fully verify one quote about community solidarity from the video game Cyberpunk.
items.title: Yale Scholar Julián Posada on the Invisible Data Workers Behind AI and Platform Exploitation

items.summary: Tech Policy Press fellow Lam Le, based in Hanoi, attended a conference held in Bangkok on November 22, 2026: the Second Regional Networking Visit for Platform Workers in Asia. The event was organized by the Just Economy and Labor Institute (JELI) and Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung (FES) Thailand. At the conference, Le met with workers and organizers while observing their discussions about organizing efforts aimed at winning recognition and labor rights for platform workers. She spoke with Justin Hendrix about her observations and shared recordings from delivery riders, remote outsourcing workers, artists, trade unionists, and researchers across India, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, and Thailand describing how they are organizing to secure these rights. A transcript of the episode is forthcoming.
items.title: Asia's Gig Workers Unite Across Borders to Fight for Rights

items.summary: In a forum post titled 'Let's normalise longer post-graduation job searching,' Adwin Lau Yu Tan, an 18-year-old Year 2 junior college student in Singapore, argues that the expectation of quickly securing employment after graduation is unrealistic. The piece references statistics indicating that Singaporean graduates are taking longer on average to find work following graduation and projects that future searches may extend even further. Lau contends that familial discussions and social support continue to promote rapid job placement, an image he attributes partly to schoolteachers as well, describing this expectation as unsustainable in reality. He urges young people to prepare for a lengthened search by productively using the interim period through volunteering, courses, and short-term jobs, while calling on society to accept the shift and acknowledge its difficulties. Lau frames his proposal around making the transition to independent income easier rather than attempting to shorten the employment gap.
items.title: Singaporean Junior College Student Calls for Normalising Longer Post-Graduation Job Searches

items.summary: In response to Esther Yeo's letter questioning an over-emphasis on perfection in school-based examination marking, Ong Kong Hong of the Ministry of Education (MOE) explained that both science curriculum design and national examinations are intended to assess students' conceptual understanding and their ability to apply concepts across contexts. He stated that markers award points for demonstrated understanding rather than penalising missing keywords or imperfect diagrams when overall responses clearly reflect concept mastery; he cited a shared circuit question, noting that a parallel arrangement of bulbs would indicate comprehension of how an electrical system functions in context. On school-based assessments specifically, the MOE noted these are managed at the school level to align with their formative purpose and lower stakes, including mark scheme design and standardisation for consistency. He added that the ministry does not supply schools with mark schemes for such assessments, but acknowledged the specific school had already addressed Yeo's feedback directly. The response concluded by affirming MOE's ongoing provision of professional development to strengthen teachers' assessment literacy while framing continued support as aimed at fostering a love of learning in students.
items.title: MOE Clarifies Marking Practices Aim to Reward Conceptual Understanding Over Perfection

items.summary: Ben Mann argues that modern large language models are essentially compressors trained on vast data, and that progress in training these compressors—measured by perplexity or cross-entropy loss—is the key indicator of advances in general intelligence. Perplexity measures how well a model predicts the next token, with lower values indicating better prediction; OpenAI tracks it as log-perplexity on an internal held-out codebase dataset for consistency across models. The text reports that GPT-2 set early state-of-the-art perplexity and enabled coherent paragraphs, while later models showed corresponding capability leaps: GPT-3 learned in context from few examples, GPT-3.5 reached a log-perplexity of approximately 0.99 to enable fluent conversation as the basis for ChatGPT, GPT-4 achieved about 0.91 with productive chain-of-thought reasoning, and models below 0.8 have produced transformative capabilities in cybersecurity and mathematics—though these emergent abilities were not predictable from the thresholds themselves. Mann notes that while downstream benchmarks saturate quickly as AI accelerates its own development—including a steep loss acceleration visible on OpenAI's plot attributed mostly to long-term research rather than automation—the pretraining metric is expected to remain informative, with transformative capabilities anticipated in the 0.68-0.7 log-perplexity window and possibly an avalanche of fundamental pretraining advances by 2027 if AI participates more in algorithmic research. He proposes that frontier developers jointly establish shared evaluation norms, red-team safety cases before first use, transparency standards, and common limits based on perplexity not to be crossed until monitoring capabilities reach a concrete milestone such as a successor to chain-of-thought monitors. The proposal faces four challenges: difficulty comparing across labs due to differing datasets and data mixtures; detachment from actionable tasks since perplexity does not directly correspond to any specific goal; failure to account for advances outside pretraining, notably that chain-of-thought reasoning increases capabilities without reducing model perplexity; and an unknown floor because a loss of 0 is unattainable while the inherent entropy of the data remains undetermined. Mann concludes that despite these challenges, perplexity has proven consistent over time as many teams optimize it for general intelligence gains.
items.title: OpenAI Proposes Perplexity as a Shared Metric for Tracking and Pacing AI Progress

items.summary:
In a self-conducted test published under the byline of Polly Hudson, an author manually disabled AI features on her iPhone—switching off Apple Intelligence in settings, marking Siri as unassisted, and deselecting suggested replies to texts and emails—but reported that proposed responses continued to appear. Bored during bus travel, she deliberately answered messages from her husband using these suggestions to determine whether he would notice the artificial origin; according to the account, he did not detect a difference even when prompted about it.

The text states that once the AI detected its own usage patterns, it escalated by generating increasingly personalized replies, including one ending with a nickname unique to their relationship. The author concluded that these suggestions were specific rather than generic because they reflected her actual communication style—describing herself as 'cheesy,' prone to exclamation marks, and characterized by British humor ('bantz'). She interpreted this impersonation as evidence of her own personality traits.

The account frames the experiment as a demonstration that resistance to AI is futile: she notes having used the very technology she had attempted to disable hours earlier. The piece ends with an assertion that she has since fully accepted AI integration, though no empirical verification or external corroboration of these claims is provided within the text.
items.title: Polly Hudson's Experiment Reveals Apple Intelligence Generates Personalized Suggested Text Responses

items.summary: Number theorist Ken Ono explains why he remains committed to mathematics even as AI-assisted tools produce major results, including Levent Alpöge's Claude-collaborated proof of the Riemann hypothesis (certified by Lean and Mathlib) announced on 20 November. Leading Epoch AI's FrontierMath number theory team in May 2025, Ono observed an unreleased ChatGPT model compute all moments of Tamagawa numbers of elliptic curves. He now works as Founding Mathematician at Axiom Math (on leave from the University of Virginia), where his team uses Lean to formalize and verify proofs; they released a complete 43.1 million-line Lean formalization of the classification of finite simple groups, which also exposed an error in a published route to a key theorem that their alternative argument addressed under 24 days of work. Ono attributes staying to personal factors—his late father's comparison of AI-assisted discovery to Ramanujan—and acknowledges he cannot offer reassurance to younger mathematicians who lack his accumulated opportunities (35 PhD students advised, 17 postdocs). He shares concerns raised by the Fields Medalists' declaration 'A Severe Misalignment of AI in Mathematics,' including rushed announcements and inadequate attribution, and calls for universities, journals, employers, funders, and students to shape what is rewarded while decisions remain open. As a mentor he insists on room to struggle with mathematics, asking what young mathematicians understood or originated rather than substituting access to powerful systems.
items.title: Ken Ono Stays in Mathematics Despite AI-Assisted Proofs While Advocating for Human-Centered Practices

items.summary:
E-commerce platform Cleverbridge disclosed that hackers breached its systems and stole customers' payment card information, including credit card numbers, expiration dates, and CVV/CVC security codes. The company detected unauthorized activity on November 4, 2026, temporarily took its systems offline to contain the breach, then brought all systems back online later that same day before determining a third party had copied stored payment card data. Cleverbridge began notifying affected customers on November 20, warning them of stolen payment details used for purchases through its platform.

While public disclosure confirmed theft without specifying which card details were compromised—referring customers to individual notifications—a breach notification shared with BleepingComputer revealed the stolen information included payment card numbers, expiration dates, and CVV/CVC codes. The notification explicitly stated that no other personal data (such as names, contact, or billing details) was copied, though it redacted the last four digits of affected cards.

The company has not disclosed how attackers gained access to its platform, how long they remained in systems, or how many customers were impacted—information BleepingComputer requested but Cleverbridge did not respond to. Of particular concern is the theft of CVV/CVC codes used to verify transactions. The incident was confirmed as not a ransomware attack, with no encrypted systems.

Cleverbridge notified data protection authorities, law enforcement, payment card networks, and payment partners about the breach. It engaged TransUnion's Cyberscout to distribute notifications and provide affected customers with complimentary credit monitoring and fraud assistance. Affected customers were advised to review statements for unauthorized transactions and contact their card issuers.

The text notes that Cleverbridge serves numerous technology brands including Red Hat, SUSE, Tenable, Veeam, Jamf, Sony, and Parallels, though it has not identified which of these businesses' customers were affected. The final section contains unrelated promotional content for Adaptive Security's email scanning service.
items.title: Cleverbridge Data Breach: Hackers Stole Credit Card Numbers and CVV Codes

items.summary: Australia's government aims to develop hydropower and Pumped Hydro Energy Storage (PHES) under its Powering Australia Plan, which targets 82 per cent renewable electricity by 2030 and net-zero emissions by 2050. The Australian Energy Market Operator expects storage demand to rise significantly as intermittent wind and solar power requires long-duration dispatchable storage; a draft 2026 Integrated System Plan estimates the country will need 27 GW of storage by 2030 and 55 GW by 2050. Australia currently operates around 8.5 GW of traditional and pumped hydropower across over 120 stations, providing between 5 per cent and 7 per cent of electricity, while an identified practical capacity exceeds 124 GW at potential project sites.
items.title: Snowy 2.0 Cost Balloons as Australia Pursues Hydropower Expansion

items.summary: Japanese material handling company Tadano has released the V320RC, a compact battery-electric wheeled pick-and-carry crane with a maximum lifting capacity of 35 tonnes. Developed in collaboration with NMG Italia and tested at that firm's job sites plus during setup operations at Marmomac in Verona, the machine is now available for purchase. The V320RC measures approximately 5 m long, 2.15 m wide, and 2.4 m tall, and runs on a 120V lithium-ion battery pack rated at 1,120 Ah (about 134 kWh). Its gross vehicle weight exceeds 31,150 kg (~34.5 short tons) and includes about 9,500 kg of removable counterweights to ease transport; a new hydraulic system pairs a variable-displacement pump with an electro-hydraulic control valve for precision and responsiveness while reducing energy use. NMG Italia reports the crane delivers roughly 50% better productivity than competing electric cranes under equivalent workloads, along with enough battery capacity for several days of operation between charges. The text notes that these performance claims are drawn from field testing by NMG Italia rather than independent verification.
items.title: Tadano launches 35-ton V320RC wheeled electric pick-and-carry crane

items.summary: The text presents NRDC's framing that increasing loss frequency and severity are outpacing insurers' ability to price and absorb them, which the organization attributes in part to climate change. This dynamic is said to drive higher premiums, reduced coverage availability, and insurer withdrawal from certain markets, thereby raising property ownership costs and exposing individuals, businesses, and communities to greater physical and financial risk. NRDC characterizes insurance as both a critical safety net for recovering from losses and a component of community resilience that supports faster recovery, continued investment, and adaptation when functioning effectively. The organization's director of insurance and financial risk, Alfonso Pating, is cited as explaining how homeowner's insurance works and why climate change makes it unaffordable. NRDC links associated reports on the insurability crisis to housing resilience and adaptation strategies.
items.title: NRDC Frames Rising Insurance Costs as a Climate-Driven Affordability Crisis

items.summary:
Tesla CEO Elon Musk denied affiliation with the MAGA movement during a New York Times DealBook Summit interview, though he did not apologize for his prior political support. CleanTechnica frames this denial as an early stage of what it calls a longer recovery process, arguing that accountability is approaching through Congress rather than spiritual means.

The article's central claim concerns SpaceX satellite services to Ukraine. According to the text, Musk took credit for providing "free" Starlink communications aid after Russia's 2014 invasion of Donbas and its 2022 assault on Kyiv failed militarily. CleanTechnica disputes this characterization with several figures: a later assessment attributed about 85% of initial terminal costs to other sources including USAID, while Poland and other groups contributed an estimated 30% of connectivity costs. The Belfer Center for International Affairs at Harvard concluded in 2023 that the U.S. government likely agreed to pay some or all ongoing operational costs.

The article states that SpaceX made unilateral decisions restricting Ukraine's use of the technology, with CEO Gwynne Shotwell asserting it was never intended "for offensive purposes." Musk reportedly further restricted service in October when he, Trump, or both reduced satellite support. In response, incoming House Intelligence Committee Chair Jim Himes (D-CT) sent a letter dated November 20 demanding an in-person briefing from senior SpaceX officers and warning that all present and future U.S. government contracts with SpaceX are at risk.

The text notes the Republican congressional majority is expected to end on January 3, when a Democratic majority takes over. It attributes ongoing service interruptions partly to Trump's engagement with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping during the same period. No charts or quantitative comparisons suitable for visualization were stated in the article.
items.title: Incoming Democratic Majority Threatens to Void SpaceX Contracts Over Starlink Service Disruptions in Ukraine

items.summary: A weekly tech roundup reports that VC deals involving NVIDIA reached $219.5 billion year to date in 2026, according to PitchBook's nine-page report; these seven frontier labs accounted for 80.3% of that value while representing just 6.4% of deal count. The report notes Jensen Huang departed as CEO on November 12 and CFO Colette Kress serves as interim during the leadership search, introducing uncertainty around relationship-driven mega-rounds. European tech investment is projected to rise from $50 billion in 2025 to $81 billion in 2026 per a 126-page report, making it the second-best year on record after the $94 billion peak in 2021; thirteen billion-dollar rounds already raised $22 billion (37% of total investment) and set a European record. Isomorphic Labs led this week's hottest deals with a $5B Series C co-led by Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital, followed by Genesis AI ($500M), Science Corporation ($400M), Model ML ($250M), Corma ($125M), Noeri ($110M), Variational ($110M), Boltz ($110M), BrightAI ($97M), and Linq ($90M). The roundup also cites a January 2026 survey of 150 IT and security decision-makers finding that 69% said security concerns slowed agent adoption while only 27% considered their identity systems fully equipped to govern agents at scale. These figures are drawn from multiple sources (PitchBook, MenloVC, NTTData) with varying sample scopes—for example, Stripe's SaaS Index covers roughly 72,000 mostly self-serve businesses excluding AI companies and most large public enterprise vendors—so the data should be treated as source-specific rather than comprehensive. The text is a promotional newsletter that mixes these figures with event promotions (Agentic Strategy Summit), job listings, and discounted resource offerings.
items.title: NVIDIA-Backed Deals Reached $219.5B in 2026, Leading a Week of Tech Funding and Investment Data

items.summary: Peter Walker of The Times reports that Theresa May, appearing on BBC One around 9:45am Sunday in an awkward defense of the EU exit, evoked a return to roughly 2018 for viewers. He frames this as emblematic of a problem facing her party: although pushing back against closer ties with the EU is reflexive for Conservatives, Andy Burnham's decision to pursue such ties returns them to what he calls their own unhappy place. Walker notes that May's earlier attempts to secure a unifying departure deal involved repeated humiliations, including what he describes as the heaviest ever parliamentary defeat for a British PM when the Commons rejected her Brexit plan by a majority of 230. He contrasts this with Kemi Badenoch's party, which seven years and four prime ministers after Boris Johnson's "get Brexit done" election triumph has opted to do less of what David Cameron called "banging on about Europe," instead focusing on policy areas such as the economy, social security, and defence. Walker attributes this caution partly to ardent Tory Brexiters struggling to articulate tangible benefits from the referendum in the intervening decade beyond niche constitutional points, and he reports that May did not argue Brexit had been a success, saying it was impossible to know given events like Covid and Russia's invasion of Ukraine while adding she does not think Britain's state today is about whether or not they left the EU. He cites polling suggesting a clear majority of Britons view Brexit as both a failure and a mistake in the first place, with similar support for rejoining the EU depending on pre-conditions; he attributes this partly to demographic churn involving the death of disproportionately older leave voters replaced by younger people with more positive views about the EU. A new constituency-level poll Walker references found that among 632 Commons seats in England, Scotland, and Wales, voters in 512 areas would rejoin the EU (with 47 too close to call), while just 73 — slightly over 11% of the total — still want to stay out. He notes Burnham's Makerfield seat is among previously leave-backing areas that now support rejoining, and reports Badenoch will lambast the PM when he sets out his new EU deal in parliament on Monday, with deputy Alex Burghart promising a future Tory government would unpick it. Walker concludes that while Europe remains contested for Conservatives, it is no longer their defining political thread or source of decades-long division.
items.title: Theresa May's Brexit endorsement prompts Conservatives to refocus away from Europe

items.summary:
A district court in The Hague ruled that Chinese automaker BYD's seven-seat plug-in hybrid Ti7 SUV infringes on Jaguar Land Rover's (JLR) EU design rights, banning the vehicle from sale across the European Union. The ruling followed legal action launched by JLR earlier this year after BYD announced it was taking orders for the model from UK customers and reported bailiffs seizing digital records from BYD offices shortly before Friday's decision. Judge preliminary relief determined that "the characteristic and distinctive elements of the design are reflected in the BYD Ti7." The ban takes effect one week after the ruling, though the judge noted BYD has no concrete plans to market the vehicle in the EU and ruled the court lacks jurisdiction over BYD's UK activities.

The Ti7, which has been on sale in China since last September, is a boxy SUV priced at £47,995 in the UK—more than £20,000 cheaper than JLR's Defender—with deliveries scheduled from January 2027. Motoring outlets have compared it to the Land Rover Defender; BBC Top Gear magazine described it as the "Chinese Defender clone." BYD stated it strongly disagrees with the ruling and will appeal, arguing the vehicle is the result of independent design work that infringes none of JLR's rights.

The court also prohibited BYD from producing the Ti7 at its new Szeged factory in Hungary until the case resolves. The decision marks a rare instance of European automakers pursuing design-right infringement in court; while many traditional makers have long complained about Chinese competitors copying designs, few cases had reached trial. JLR previously won against Jiangling Motors Corporation over a copycat vehicle in 2019 after a three-year battle.

The ruling's scope is limited: it does not extend to BYD's UK operations or its China sales of the Ti7, which began last September.
items.title: Dutch Court Bans BYD From Selling Ti7 SUV in EU After JLR Design Infringement Claim

items.summary: The COP31 climate summit in Türkiye collapsed on Sunday without reaching a final agreement, marking the first unsuccessful conclusion since the 2009 Copenhagen meeting. Negotiations stretched to their longest in three decades before summit president Murat Kurum acknowledged that delegates could not even agree on what the document's overarching goal should be, stating there was no consensus and therefore the decisions had not been adopted. The breakdown effectively ended a 2023 Dubai consensus on phasing out fossil fuels from the global economy; while successive energy crises accelerated fuel pivots in some importing countries, they reinforced others' conviction that more investment is needed in legacy energy systems for security and affordability. Overlapping wars and US President Donald Trump's foreign policy have further undermined multilateralism, which a negotiating process requiring consensus depends on — a requirement former Vice President Al Gore criticized as 'insane.' The draft decision included new calls for carbon capture seen by many teams as a cover for extending fossil fuel lifespans; it was supported by the Arab Group (including the UAE), China, India, and Japan, but adamantly opposed by least-developed-countries blocs as well as the UK and EU. Meanwhile, more than two dozen minor emitters adopted transition-away-from-fossil-fuels guidelines and nearly 90 countries pledged to accelerate electrification during COP31. The text notes that climate action became a casualty of energy turmoil rather than presenting this collapse as an inevitable outcome, and quotes Panama's former climate envoy Juan Carlos Monterrey Gómez asserting the green economy will win because it is cheaper and creates jobs rather than through negotiated texts — framing these smaller-group agreements as partial successes within a deeply fragmented process. The article presents the fragmentation as evidence of declining universal agreement on global energy pathways while acknowledging that real-world economic forces operate independently of UN-brokered summits, without establishing whether this collapse will ultimately prevent or merely delay broader climate action.
items.title: COP31 Climate Summit Collapsed Without Agreement

items.summary: The Federation of Indian Pilots (FIP) asked the civil aviation ministry to order an immediate financial and safety review of SpiceJet, warning that prolonged distress could undermine employee welfare, maintenance quality, operational reliability, and aviation safety. FIP president Captain C S Randhawa requested that the DGCA assess the airline's cash and working capital, outstanding salaries, statutory and airport dues, fuel payments, lessor liabilities, serviceable aircraft and crew levels, flight duty time compliance, engine support, critical spares, insurance, and the source, timing, and proposed use of a board-approved ₹5,500-crore fundraise. If SpiceJet could not demonstrate capacity to run its approved schedule safely, FIP argued its operations should be regulated in the interest of passenger safety. The federation attributed the crisis to weak working capital, lower fleet utilisation, continued fixed costs, accumulated dues, repeated reliance on fundraising, and rising dollar-denominated lease rentals as the rupee depreciated; it cited CARE Ratings for aviation turbine fuel accounting for about 36% of SpiceJet's overall costs in FY 2024-25. FIP warned that delayed salaries could cause financial anxiety, stress, fatigue, and reduced concentration among pilots and other safety-critical staff, while unpaid dues to lessors, airport operators, oil companies, maintenance providers, and vendors—some placed on cash-and-carry arrangements—had grounded a substantial part of the fleet and disrupted published schedules. FIP noted SpiceJet's domestic market share fell from about 21% in 2014 to nearly 0.6% in October 2026 amid persistent cash-flow problems, accumulated liabilities, and difficulty meeting daily financial commitments. The DGCA issued a show-cause notice on 17 November 2026 over operational disruptions, non-compliance, unpaid dues, grounded aircraft, and the absence of a credible recovery plan, giving SpiceJet seven days to respond. FIP stressed that although the ₹5,500-crore fundraise's timing and use are critical to revival, the problems appear systemic and cannot be resolved through short-term infusions alone; it urged that employee remuneration be treated as a priority operational obligation during financial stress and proposed mandatory annual health/safety-risk assessments for all scheduled airlines with quarterly monitoring for distressed carriers. The federation also called for lower, uniform VAT on aviation turbine fuel—potentially under the GST framework—and temporary relief or deferral of airport charges such as landing, parking, navigation, and ground-handling fees. These claims are drawn from FIP's letter to the civil aviation minister; figures like market share and cost percentages reflect reported estimates rather than independently verified data.
items.title: FIP Urges Government Intervention in SpiceJet Over Financial and Safety Concerns

items.summary: Saurav Das, co-convener of the Cockroach Janata Party, announced on Sunday that the party's flagship initiative, the Cockroach Club, would provide a physical space where young Indians could discuss politics and society, engage with intellectual traditions, read, watch films, attend cultural performances, question conventional thought, and relax. According to Das's explanatory post on X, the club aims to combine recreation with intellectual engagement so that visitors can learn and unwind in the same setting while developing their own perspectives about India's future. The announcement describes intended functions of the project but does not provide details such as a launch date, location, funding sources, or membership plans.
items.title: Cockroach Janata Party's Saurav Das Announces Cockroach Club Plan for India's Youth

items.summary: In southern Lebanon, the Kadouh family returned in July 2025 to their home in Zawtar al-Gharbiyah — a village they had lived in for decades and built themselves after two decades of work abroad. Their return coincided with what they describe as the first test of a U.S.-brokered plan under which Israeli forces withdrew from south Lebanon and the Lebanese army took over, an arrangement intended to keep Iran-backed Hezbollah out of the area following its resumption of cross-border rocket fire in solidarity with Hamas after October 2023. Upon returning, Atef Kadouh and his wife Soumaya Yaghi found their house occupied by Israeli soldiers before being set on fire; scorched walls bore Hebrew names written in blue marker near a work roster, appliances had bullet holes, furniture was pushed off the second-floor balcony, burned food packets with Hebrew writing lay on the floor, and soot from a scorched ceiling dripped onto an 18-month-old grandson's bedroom. The family reported no running water or electricity because solar panels were destroyed, that Lebanese army personnel dismantled explosives left behind in their house, and that bulldozers had uprooted trees — including pine nut cash crops — while the garage and tractor were demolished. Israel acknowledged destroying more than 20,000 homes across its self-declared security zone along the border since a ceasefire this year but declined to explain why these specific structures were damaged or burned, stating that military policy bars burning homes or leaving explosives. The Israeli military attributed killings of medical personnel to militants posing as paramedics without providing proof and did not respond to questions noting five medics were killed at a burial rather than in an ambulance; Lebanon's Health Ministry said Israel had killed more than 135 first responders and medical staff over the past two years, including Atef's son Adel, who volunteered as an ambulance driver and was killed on March 28. Kadouh reported that his sons serve in the Lebanese army and national security services but have never been allowed to work because he says the force is deliberately underequipped to avoid presenting a threat to Israel; he said villagers feel abandoned by their own government, Hezbollah allies, and outsiders alike.
items.title: Lebanese villagers return to destroyed homes as Israeli forces withdraw from Zawtar al-Gharbiyah

items.summary: A review of the personal independence payment (Pip) system, co-led by social security minister Stephen Timms and disability rights advocates Clenton Farquharson and Sharon Brennan, is expected this week—possibly as early as Tuesday—to recommend overhauling Pip rather than scrapping it. The interim report in July and further findings in September established a consensus that the benefit was 'no longer fit for purpose,' with draft recommendations calling mainly for changes to the assessment system so conditions varying over time are better accounted for, while retaining the scheme across all ages. Cash payments were described as the foundation of any reformed benefit, which would remain non-means tested and could include in-kind awards such as services, aids or training alongside cash. This stands in contrast to a separate report by Alan Milburn on youth worklessness, published last week, which called for entirely scrapping Pip for adults under 25—alongside universal credit health benefit payments—and replacing it with an 'additional cost allowance' within a broader network of job-based support; that proposal would cut £3.6bn from spending on young people. Government officials rejected the notion of a clash between the two reviews, noting Milburn's review was commissioned after Timms' process had begun and that about 90% of Pip claimants are over 25. Some members of the Timms steering group reportedly expressed concern over the scale of Milburn's proposals; one source told The Guardian that 'some members are really concerned.' Prime minister Andy Burnham faces pressure from Conservatives to reduce working-age benefit costs while rejecting what he called 'crude cuts,' and ministers will need to decide next steps on a sensitive subject after Keir Starmer abandoned planned changes in 2025 following a Labour rebellion. The Timms review's remit did not include the cost of Pip or potential spending cuts, so much of its longer-term detail would be decided by ministers before legislation is considered next year.
items.title: Timms Pip Review Expected to Recommend Overhaul Rather Than Scrapping Benefit for Under-25s

items.summary: Libya's eastern Government of National Stability (GNS) said an explosion on a Russian ship docked at the Benghazi naval base port was caused by a suspected drone attack. The blast occurred at dawn Sunday while the vessel had stopped for fuel and supplies en route back to Russia, according to Libyan state media citing the GNS; Moscow has not yet commented. Satellite imagery reviewed by BBC Verify shows a boat on fire at 0547 GMT with a later image of the same ship partially submerged, and social-media videos geolocated by BBC Verify show the vessel engulfed in flames during darkness. The eastern government said there were no casualties and that the site was secured. It described the incident as an attack inside a Libyan port under an existing maritime agreement, condemning it as a violation of maritime safety and sovereignty while asserting Libya is not party to the Russia-Ukraine war or any conflict beyond its borders. Authorities are coordinating with Russian counterparts to determine the source and responsibility for the suspected attack. Separately, Libya's internationally recognised Government of National Unity (GNU) in Tripoli warned against hosting foreign forces and using facilities, citing fears over involving ports and civilian assets in external conflicts.
items.title: Suspected Drone Attack Exploded a Russian Ship at Benghazi Port

items.summary:
Libya's eastern-based government, backed by military commander Khalifa Haftar, reported that an explosion aboard a Russian ship docked in the port of Benghazi was caused by a suspected drone attack. The vessel had reportedly stopped to refuel and resupply on its way back to Russia under maritime cooperation agreements between the two countries. Initial investigations indicated the blast occurred onboard the ship, with reports suggesting it was struck from above within a few kilometres of the target; no one has claimed responsibility for the strike.

No deaths were reported as of the reporting, though injuries occurred and their number and nationalities remained unknown at the time. The eastern Libyan authority condemned the attack as a violation of Libya's sovereignty and stated it would pursue legal and diplomatic measures against those responsible, while confirming port facilities had been secured after the fire was brought under control.

The incident is linked to Ukrainian long-range operations, with reports that a small unit of Ukrainian special forces based in Misrata has coordinated drone attacks on Russian tankers and transport ships. If confirmed as a successful strike on a Russian warship, it would represent one of Ukraine's most significant naval successes during the conflict, though analysts noted the attack extends fighting beyond eastern Europe into regions where civilians could be affected.

Separately, Finland reported that its border guard was working with Russia and Estonia to extinguish a fire aboard the cargo ship Sparta II in the Baltic Sea. The Finnish military said the strike on Saturday was probably carried out by Ukraine; the vessel had been damaged west of Gogland Island before drifting into Finnish waters where 16 crew members were evacuated, one slightly injured. Visible flames had subsided by Sunday with operations focused on cooling containers and stabilizing the ship.

The reporting notes that Kyiv has directed waves of drones toward Russia's Leningrad region this year, some straying into Baltic airspace, raising concerns about spillover onto NATO territory. Estonian Navy commander Ivo Värk stated the risk of further attacks in the Gulf of Finland could not be ruled out, and Finnish authorities reported detecting a strike on another Russian warship earlier that week during Ukrainian drone operations.

The text attributes all claims to their respective sources without independent verification: no immediate claim of responsibility was made for either attack, and casualty figures remained unconfirmed. The analysis reflects the divided nature of Libya's governance and Russia's reliance on eastern Libyan ports.
items.title: Suspected Drone Attack Damages Russian Ship at Benghazi Port; Separate Baltic Vessel Fire Continues

items.summary: International climate negotiations in Antalya, Turkey, broke down on Sunday when nearly 200 countries failed to agree on moving away from fossil fuels. European Union negotiators refused to finalize an agreement that did not mention the transition off coal and natural gas—the primary drivers of warming—and walked out; Panama and island states such as the Marshall Islands also objected afterward. EU climate chief Wopke Hoekstra said the bloc could not accept a deal omitting fossil fuels while heading toward a 1.5-degree overshoot, calling it unacceptable. The collapse occurred at the first U.N. summit with scientific consensus that the world would surpass the 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) limit agreed in 2015; burning oil, gas, and coal accounts for roughly 73% of global emissions. Crossing this threshold is expected to intensify hurricanes and heat waves, and a best-case scenario of 1.7 or 1.8 degrees would require immediate cuts reducing emissions by 45% by 2035—changes scientists say demand sharply reduced fossil fuel use. Mohamed Adow of Power Shift Africa described the rejected decision as insufficient to protect vulnerable populations that have contributed least yet suffer most.
items.title: Climate talks in Antalya collapse over fossil fuel language

items.summary: On November 22 at the KC Stadium, Hull City secured their first Premier League win since August with a 2-0 victory over promoted Brighton & Hove Albion. Oli McBurnie scored both goals in stoppage time after Joao Costinha was sent off for a second yellow card late in the match, and manager Sergej Jakirovic praised his side's collective effort following what he described as an almost three-month wait since their previous win. Hull goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis made five saves in the first half to preserve parity against Brighton's high-intensity pressure before Hull grew into the contest after halftime; Jakirovic credited Tzolakis with saving them four or five times and noted greater stability in the second half.
items.title: Hull City's Injury-Time Double Ends Winless Run in 2-0 Victory Over Brighton

items.summary: The Confederation of African Football announced during its congress in Nigeria that six venues have been chosen to host matches at next year's Africa Cup of Nations finals, a 24-team tournament co-hosted by Kenya, Tanzania, and Uganda. The competition is scheduled to run from June 19 to July 17, though the venue for the final remains undecided. Kenya will contribute one venue in Nairobi, where the new Talanta Stadium with a capacity of 60,000 is set to open in January. Tanzania's three venues are located in Arusha, Dar es Salaam, and Zanzibar. Uganda will use two stadiums: the Mandela National Stadium in Kampala and the newly built Hoima City Stadium.
items.title: Six Venues Selected for Co-Hosted Africa Cup of Nations Finals

items.summary: On the sidelines of the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, China, CMG's He Yanke conducted an interview with Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori as part of a special edition of 'Leaders Talk.' The conversation explored several topics: the significance of APEC for Peru and its potential role in connecting economies and expanding trade within the Asia-Pacific region; the growing economic and trade relationship between China and Peru, including opportunities arising from the Port of Chancay and the upgraded China-Peru Free Trade Agreement; and Peru's broader efforts to attract foreign investment, develop renewable energy, expand tourism, and strengthen its position as a logistics hub for South America. The interview was framed by an editorial note posing questions about APEC's role in facilitating regional cooperation and deepening bilateral partnerships.
items.title: Exclusive Interview: Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori Discusses APEC and China-Peru Economic Ties

items.summary:
The International Monetary Fund projects that Israel will become the world's 25th-largest economy by end of 2026, with nominal GDP reaching approximately $747 billion to overtake Sweden and Ireland. This projection is set against a backdrop of ongoing conflict, as more than 700 participants—including over 200 European guests—gather for the ELNET Jerusalem Summit (November 22–24) to discuss closer cooperation on security, technology, research and trade. The IMF forecasts 4.5% economic growth in 2026; the Bank of Israel is more optimistic with 5.6% this year and 7.5% in 2027 (figures that include overseas production), though domestic-only estimates are lower at 3.4% for 2026 and 5.1% for 2027.

The article attributes Israel's economic performance largely to its technology sector, which the Israel Innovation Authority's State of High-Tech 2026 report places at 18.3% of GDP in 2025 and about 58% of exports, with strengths in cybersecurity, AI, software, semiconductors, medical tech and defence. R&D spending is cited as approximately 6.8% of GDP in 2024 (OECD), compared with around 2.3% for the EU (Eurostat). The innovation model emphasizes close ties between universities, companies, investors and government—through institutions like the Israel Innovation Authority—and a risk-tolerant entrepreneurial culture supported by venture capital.

The text notes that this development occurred despite military operations, reservist mobilisation, labour shortages and high defence spending. It cautions that defence expenditure should not be equated with prosperity, as it strains resources for education, transport and healthcare; the OECD's Economic Survey of Israel 2025 highlights associated challenges.

Remaining risks include a temporary inflationary pressure from higher energy prices and supply shortages (IMF July 2026 assessment) and medium-term growth constraints from low employment among ultra-Orthodox Jewish men and Arab Israeli women. The piece concludes by drawing lessons for Europe—prioritising innovation, strengthening university-business cooperation, improving startup financing, cross-industry collaboration and international orientation—and flags that closer European-Israeli ties remain politically contentious in parts of Europe due to disagreements over Palestinian policy.
items.title: IMF Projects Israel Will Become World's 25th-Largest Economy in 2026 Amid Tech-Driven Growth

items.summary:
A powerful explosion aboard a Russian vessel docked at Libya's eastern port of Benghazi on Sunday prompted local authorities to suspect a drone attack, though no group or government has claimed responsibility and the incident remains officially unconfirmed. Officials from Libya's eastern administration stated that the ship was in port for refuelling and resupply before returning to Russia; while early reports suggested a fire at a naval ammunition facility, they later clarified that the blast originated on the vessel itself. No casualties were reported, but emergency crews responded to contain the blaze, which residents were advised to avoid until firefighters brought it under control. The eastern government announced plans for a joint investigation with Russian officials.

Naval analysts have provisionally identified the ship as the Russian missile corvette Merkury, though Libyan authorities did not confirm this or disclose cargo details. Although no evidence publicly links Ukraine to the Benghazi explosion, its timing has drawn attention amid reports of other maritime incidents: a drone strike on a Russian cargo vessel in the eastern Baltic Sea near Finnish waters on Saturday (attributed by Finland's military but unconfirmed by Kyiv), and damage to a Russian LNG carrier off Libya's coast in March that Putin blamed on Ukraine. These events have raised concerns about attacks targeting Russia's shadow fleet, which transports energy exports while evading sanctions.

The incident has heightened security anxieties around the vulnerability of commercial shipping routes, port facilities, and maritime logistics networks outside traditional conflict zones, with risks to port workers, coastal communities, and the marine environment. Libya's internationally recognised Government of National Unity in Tripoli warned against using its ports for foreign military operations amid concerns that the country could become a battleground.

The investigation faces significant uncertainties: whether the explosion was deliberate, who carried it out, and what cargo the vessel transported remain unanswered pending examination of physical and technical evidence. The outcome may reveal broader implications if a drone strike is confirmed regarding the potential impact on North African ports and maritime facilities.
items.title: Suspected Drone Strike Hits Russian Ship at Libya's Benghazi Port

items.summary: At the FIFA U-17 World Cup in Doha, Qatar, Uganda's Cranes were held to a goalless draw by Ecuador in their second Group B match on Sunday. Despite an energetic attacking display and sustained pressure against an Ecuador side that frequently used its wings, Uganda could not convert efforts into goals. Midfielder Muhoozi Henry was named player of the match for his contributions to keeping the team competitive. A near miss in the first half was denied when a goal was ruled out after defender Cuadrado made contact with goalkeeper Lukyamuzi Ashraf. Joseph Dorongin and Jemba Ukasha received yellow cards in the 39th and 60th minutes respectively. Coach Laryea Kingston said Uganda aimed to keep possession, used substitutions to add fresh legs to midfield, acknowledged that another striker could have been added for a winner, and praised both teams faced so far. He made his first change in the 39th minute by replacing Ismail Fahad with Junior Ofoyrwth, then brought on Arafat Ibanda, Arnold Kayemba, and Babi Shakur in three further substitutions at the 73rd minute. Muhoozi credited his teammates for helping him earn the award and described the contest as tough. Uganda now face New Caledonia in their final group match, where a win is needed to secure progression to the round of 32.
items.title: Uganda Draw Goalless Match With Ecuador at FIFA U-17 World Cup

The United Nations COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Turkey collapsed on Sunday after delegates failed to reach an agreement on addressing climate change. European nations and many smaller countries vulnerable to climate disasters rejected the draft deal, arguing it removed crucial protections while favouring fossil fuel-exporting states—oil, gas, and coal producers identified as the primary driver of global warming. COP31 President and Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum acknowledged that no consensus was reached on the text, stating at the closing session in Antalya that these decisions therefore had not been adopted. He noted the presidency worked "day and night" toward a stronger outcome during an extended two-day meeting beyond its planned schedule.

Kurum confirmed there would be no new document after the fourth draft—which notably omitted any mention of fossil fuels—was rejected. The absence of an overarching agreement means climate action is likely to revert to existing frameworks, including the Paris Agreement and prior COP commitments. This outcome reflects a broader historical pattern: for roughly 25 years of UN climate talks, outcomes avoided explicitly naming fossil fuels until three years ago, when a landmark deal in oil-rich Dubai called for transitioning away from them. The Turkish-Australian proposal that followed recalled the Dubai agreement entirely, but this was insufficient to satisfy many nations and environmental groups seeking stronger protections against fossil fuel interests.
items.title: UN COP31 Climate Talks Collapse Over Fossil Fuel Protections
